citations.quote: Let $\sigma_i$ be the positive geometric Artin braid crossing in a braid rectangle whose parameter increases from bottom to top, with strand $i$ passing below and strand $i+1$ passing above. Use the bracket chart in which the over-strand runs southwest to northeast, the $A$-smoothing joins top to top and bottom to bottom with weight $A$, and the $B$-smoothing joins left to left and right to right with weight $A^{-1}$. Let $I$ be the through pairing and let $e_i$ be the pairing with a top cap and a bottom cup at positions $i,i+1$. Then the positive crossing has bracket operator $A I+A^{-1}e_i$, and the negative crossing has bracket operator $A^{-1}I+A e_i$.

For a state $S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$, let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ be the numbers of
A- and B-smoothings, and let $|S|$ be the number of closed circles in the
crossingless diagram obtained by performing all smoothings. Set
$$\delta:=-A^2-A^{-2}$$
and define the **Kauffman bracket** of $D$ by
$$\langle D\rangle:=\sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}} A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}\in\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}].$$
Because $D$ is nonempty, every complete smoothing has $|S|\ge1$, so the loop
exponent is nonnegative. A crossingless $k$-component unlink with $k\ge1$ has
bracket $\delta^{k-1}$.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

Assume full AC. If $D$ is a connected reduced alternating diagram of a knot $K$, then the library Jones polynomial has $t$-span exactly $c(K)=c(D)$, in the convention $t=A^{-4}$. The span of a nonzero Laurent polynomial is its largest exponent minus its smallest exponent.

A regular link diagram is **connected** when its underlying projection graph is connected. It is **alternating** when successive crossing visits along each component switch between overpasses and underpasses. It is **reduced** when no complementary region of the projection sphere has a crossing more than once on its boundary. A connected alternating diagram that is reduced is a **reduced alternating link diagram**.

For a link projection on $S^2$, a **checkerboard coloring** assigns one of two colors to each complementary region so that regions sharing an edge have different colors. Given such a coloring, the **black Tait graph** has one vertex for each black region and one edge for each crossing joining the two opposite black sectors at that crossing. The **white Tait graph** is defined by interchanging black and white. Loops and parallel edges are allowed.
For a connected regular link projection on $S^2$ with at least one crossing and either checkerboard coloring, both Tait graphs are connected.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ and $t$ be formal variables and $K$ a
nonempty oriented link. At each crossing of a regular diagram $D$ use the
source chart with over-strand southwest-to-northeast: A joins top and bottom
endpoints with coefficient $A$, and B joins left and right endpoints with
coefficient $A^{-1}$. A state $S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$ assigns one smoothing at every
crossing; let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count these choices and $|S|$ count the
resulting circles. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection
plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the
ambient oriented $3$-sphere. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c)=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under}),
\qquad \operatorname{wr}(D)=\sum_c\operatorname{sgn}(c),$$
$$f_K(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}
  \sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1}.$$
For an $n$-strand braid $\beta$ whose oriented closure is $K$, let
$e:B_n\to\mathbb Z$ be the homomorphism $e(\sigma_i)=1$, where $\sigma_i$
is the positive geometric Artin half twist. Let $H(n)$ be the type-A Hecke
algebra with generators $T_i$, quadratic relation $T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v$, braid
relations, and distant commutation, and let $\pi_n(\sigma_i)=T_i$. Its
normalized Markov trace $\operatorname{tr}_n$ satisfies
$\operatorname{tr}_n(1)=1$, cyclicity, tower restriction, and
$\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_n)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(x)$. Define the library
Jones value by
$$V_K(t)=s^{e(\beta)}\left(-\frac{s^2+1}{s}\right)^{n-1}
\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\Big|_{v=s^2,\,z=-1/(s^2+1),\,t=s^2},$$
where $s=t^{1/2}$. With $A=t^{-1/4}$, these values satisfy
$$V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4}).$$

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

derivations.claim: For the closure of $\sigma_1^3$, the endpoint permutation is the transposition of the two strands, hence one cycle by [F4]. The three positive crossings form a connected projection. Starting on the left bottom strand, the successive crossing visits are under, over, under; after closure the right bottom strand visits over, under, over. Thus the diagram is alternating. Its black Tait graph has two vertices and three parallel edges, while the white dual graph is a triangle. Both graphs have no loops, so no crossing repeats a region on its boundary; the diagram is reduced by [F6].

For the four-level braid with levels $\sigma_2^{-1},\sigma_1,\sigma_2^{-1},\sigma_1$, the successive endpoint orders are $[1,3,2]$, $[3,1,2]$, $[3,2,1]$, and $[2,3,1]$. The resulting endpoint permutation is the cycle $1\mapsto3\mapsto2\mapsto1$, so the closure is one knot component by [F4]. Traversing it from the first bottom strand gives crossing visits under, over; from the third bottom strand gives under, over, under; and from the second gives over, under, over. The full cyclic sequence alternates. The black Tait graph is the theta graph with two parallel edges between $u,v$ and a two-edge path $u-w-v$; it has no loops or bridges. Its dual has no loops because the primal has no bridges. Thus both color pairs at every crossing are distinct and the diagram is reduced by [F6].

If exactly $k$ of the three positive crossings use the $B$-smoothing, the states and circle counts are: $k=0$: $1$ state with $2$ circles; $k=1$: $3$ states with $1$ circle; $k=2$: $3$ states with $2$ circles; $k=3$: $1$ state with $3$ circles. Stacking through pairings and cup-cap pairings and closing the two top endpoints to the corresponding bottom endpoints gives these counts. By [F1]–[F2], the grouped contributions are $A^3\delta+3A+3A^{-1}\delta+A^{-3}\delta^2=A^{-7}-A^{-3}-A^5$. The writhe is $3$ by [F3], so [F7] gives $V_{3_1}(t)=(-A^3)^{-3}(A^{-7}-A^{-3}-A^5)\big|_{t=A^{-4}}=t+t^3-t^4$. Its span is $3$, and [F5] gives crossing number $3$.

Encode a state by four bits from bottom to top, with $0$ meaning through pairing and $1$ meaning cup-cap pairing. Let $p$ be the number of cup-cap choices at positive crossings and $q$ the number at negative crossings; [F1] gives weight exponent $2(q-p)$. Closing the pairings gives the exhaustive state data $\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{state}&\text{circles}&\text{exponent}\\0000&3&0\\0001&2&-2\\0010&2&2\\0011&1&0\\0100&2&-2\\0101&3&-4\\0110&1&0\\0111&2&-2\\1000&2&2\\1001&1&0\\1010&3&4\\1011&2&2\\1100&1&0\\1101&2&-2\\1110&2&2\\1111&1&0\end{array}$. Thus the five one-circle states contribute $5$, the eight two-circle states contribute $4(A^2+A^{-2})\delta$, and the three three-circle states contribute $(1+A^4+A^{-4})\delta^2$. Expanding $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ gives $\langle D_F\rangle=5+4(A^2+A^{-2})\delta+(1+A^4+A^{-4})\delta^2=A^8-A^4+1-A^{-4}+A^{-8}$. There are two positive and two negative crossings, so writhe is $0$ by [F3]. By [F7], $V_{4_1}(t)=t^{-2}-t^{-1}+1-t+t^2$, whose span is $4$. Applying [F5] gives crossing number $4$.

citations.quote: An oriented link $L\subset S^3$ is **split** if a smoothly embedded sphere $S\subset S^3\setminus L$ has link points in both components of $S^3\setminus S$; otherwise $L$ is **nonsplit**.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.
When the vertex set has a supplied total order, it is induced by the
simplicial-to-singular chain map of [[def-simplicial-to-singular-chain-map]],
extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.
For an arbitrary vertex set, the isomorphism is defined compatibly on its
finite subcomplexes and requires no choice principle.

derivations.claim: Linking can be computed here using finite rational chains: a rational $1$-cycle $a$ in $S^3$ bounds a rational $2$-chain $C$ by [F3], and $\operatorname{lk}(a,b)=C\mathbin{\cdot}b$ for a disjoint rational cycle $b$. Independence of $C$ follows because the difference of two choices bounds a $3$-chain by [F3], whose intersection with the closed cycle $b$ has total boundary zero. In particular linking is zero if $a$ bounds a chain disjoint from $b$, and is unchanged under a homology of $b$ in the complement of $a$. All chains involved are finite. Curves and surfaces used below can be put in finite general position: subdivide their compact parameter domains finely in finitely many coordinate neighborhoods, approximate by polygonal patches within a tubular neighborhood, perturb the finitely many vertices to avoid the finitely many nontransverse affine incidences, and smooth the patches in smaller neighborhoods. Approximation sufficiently close to the original embedded patches preserves embedding and disjointness from the compact boundary $L$. These operations use finitely many choices, and no simultaneous choices indexed by an infinite family.

We record elementary finite-surface facts needed below. Cutting the supplied presentation along a finite family of curves gives finite triangulations of its pieces. A connected triangulated surface with boundary has a graph spine: in the dual graph include a vertex for the boundary, choose a finite spanning tree rooted there, and remove triangles successively across their edge facing the already removed parent. The remaining $1$-complex is a deformation retract, and reversing these elementary collapses shows that the surface is a regular neighborhood of that graph. Consequently its rational first homology vanishes exactly when that graph is a tree, in which case its regular neighborhood is a disk, by successively removing leaf edges. Also, a two-sided simple closed curve $\gamma$ in the interior of $F$ with $[\gamma]=0$ bounds an orientable subsurface $F_0$ having $\gamma$ as its only boundary. To see this, triangulate with $\gamma$ as an edge cycle and take a rational $2$-chain bounding it using [F4]. Across edges outside $\gamma$ its coefficients agree with orientation signs. They vanish on the component touching $\partial F$ and jump by one across $\gamma$, so the nonzero component supplies precisely such an oriented $F_0$. The same coefficient argument shows that $H_1(F_0;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ is injective: any bounding chain for a cycle in $F_0$ has zero coefficients on the connected complementary surface, which touches $\partial F$.

Suppose $D$ is a compressing disk for $F$: its interior misses $F$ and its boundary $\gamma$ does not bound a disk in $F$. Its boundary is two-sided in $F$, since a collar of the disk at $\gamma$ gives a side of the normal interval bundle there. The normal transfer of a sufficiently close parallel copy of $\gamma$ misses $D$; in a collar of $\gamma$, move the parallel copy slightly in the direction tangent to $F$ and transverse to $\gamma$, and take its normal lifts still closer to that copy. Thus $\operatorname{lk}(\gamma,\tau\gamma)=0$ by step 1.1. Definiteness forces $[\gamma]=0$. Step 1.2 supplies the subsurface $F_0$ bounded by $\gamma$. It is not a disk, and hence $V=H_1(F_0;\mathbb Q)$ is nonzero and injects into $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$. Cap $F_0$ with $D$ and smooth the corner, giving a closed connected orientable embedded surface $\Sigma$. Capping the unique boundary circle does not change $H_1$, so $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)=V$.

The surface $\Sigma$ has a two-sided collar. Apply [F2] to that collar and $S^3\setminus\Sigma$. Their overlap has two components, each retracting onto $\Sigma$. By [F3], the map from the overlap's $H_0=\mathbb Q^2$ into $\mathbb Q\oplus H_0(S^3\setminus\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ is injective and has cokernel $\mathbb Q$. Hence the complement has exactly two components, and the two collar sides belong to different ones. Let $A$ and $B$ be their closures. Thickening them to open sets, [F2] and [F3] give an isomorphism $V\to H_1(A;\mathbb Q)\oplus H_1(B;\mathbb Q)$. At least one projection has nonzero kernel: if both were injective, each target would have dimension at least $\dim V>0$, contradicting that their dimensions sum to $\dim V$. Thus a nonzero $a\in V$ bounds a rational $2$-chain on one side, say in $A$. Represent $a$ by an oriented rational multicurve in $\operatorname{int}F_0$. Both of its normal pushoffs have the same linking with it: the two normal directions are joined by a half-rotation in the normal plane of each oriented curve, giving a homology of the pushoffs in its complement. The pushoff into $\operatorname{int}B$ misses the bounding chain in $A$, so that linking is zero by step 1.1. The normal transfer therefore has linking zero as well. Step 1.2 makes $a$ nonzero in $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, contradicting definiteness of $q$. Thus $F$ has no compressing disk.

By step 3.1, $F$ is incompressible. Suppose now that a splitting sphere $S$ exists. Make it transverse to $F$ by the finite perturbation of step 1.1, keeping it disjoint from $L$. Their intersection is a finite union of circles. At least one is essential in $F$: otherwise each bounds a disk in $F$, and removing the interiors of the outermost such disks leaves a connected surface containing every component of $\partial F=L$, disjoint from $S$. Its boundary would lie entirely on one side of $S$, contrary to [F1]. Choose a circle $\gamma$ innermost on $S$ among the circles essential in $F$, and let $D$ be the disk it bounds on $S$ with no other essential circle in its interior.

Every circle of $\operatorname{int}D\cap F$ bounds a disk in $F$. If there are any, choose one $\beta$ whose disk $E\subset F$ is innermost among them. Its interior misses $D$: any intersection circle in that interior would itself be inessential in $F$ and would contradict the choice. The essential curve $\gamma$ cannot lie inside $E$. Replace the disk on $D$ bounded by $\beta$ by a small parallel copy of $E$, choosing the side that joins the remainder of $D$ and smoothing its boundary. Since $\operatorname{int}E$ misses $D$, this is again an embedded disk with boundary $\gamma$. It stays disjoint from $L$ and has strictly fewer intersection circles with $F$; the replacement disk is pushed off $F$ and all circles inside the discarded disk have disappeared. Repeating this finite reduction gives an embedded disk with boundary $\gamma$ and interior disjoint from $F$. This is a compressing disk, contrary to step 3.1. The splitting sphere cannot exist, so $L$ is nonsplit.

derivations.claim: Suppose first that there is at least one crossing. Take small disjoint crossing neighborhoods and thin strips along the finitely many projection edges. Each region of the chosen color has a disk core in the complement of these strips; connectedness makes the projection a cellular graph on the sphere, so shrinking its open disk regions gives exactly these disk cores. At every crossing join the two appropriate disk cores by a narrow band with one half-twist; choose its direction so that its boundary strands have the diagram's prescribed overpass and underpass. The neighborhoods are disjoint, so the resulting surface is embedded. Its boundary is the usual height realization of $D$. Collapsing each disk to a vertex and each band to its core retracts $F$ onto the Tait graph $G$. This graph is connected by [F2], so $F$ is connected and has a supplied finite disk-and-band presentation.

Measure the signed half-twist of a band relative to the planar framing of its two disk ends; call this incidence sign $\epsilon_e$. This is the unoriented crossing incidence, not the oriented link crossing sign. At two crossings joined by a projection edge, alternation changes which branch is over, while the chosen-color sector changes sides along that edge. The two changes cancel in the half-twist chart, giving the same incidence sign at the two crossings. Since the projection graph is connected, every band has one common sign $\epsilon$. Reversing the chosen orientation of a graph edge reverses its cycle coefficient, without changing this incidence sign.

We compute the normal pairing in the disk-and-band presentation. After clearing rational denominators, represent a cycle by finitely many oriented parallel strands through each band, joined by arcs in the vertex disks; any extraneous arc pairs can be canceled inside those disks. The signed number of strands through band $e$ is its graph coefficient $a_e$. Normal transfer gives two local pushoffs of each strand, exchanged at a one-sided passage. In an untwisted planar disk the contributions of the two normal sides to the mixed-crossing count cancel. In a band with a signed half-turn, each ordered pair of an original strand and a transferred strand contributes $\epsilon_e$ to the total pairing: one normal side passes from one side of the original strand to the other during the half-turn, and the other normal side makes the complementary passage; the two mixed crossings have the same incidence sign, and the linking count is half their signed sum. Reversing either strand orientation reverses the corresponding contribution. Consequently the contribution of that band is $\epsilon_e(\sum_i s_i)(\sum_j s_j)=\epsilon_e a_e^2$, where $s_i=\pm1$ are the strand orientations. This is also a direct computation with the half-twisted strip $(u,v)\mapsto(u,v\cos(\pi u),v\sin(\pi u))$, reversing the half-turn for the other sign. The strips' end collars are included in this count; crossings of joining arcs in the planar disks cancel between the two normal sides. Linking here can be computed by the signed mixed-crossing count because a finite oriented smoothing of the first curve gives spanning disks and crossing bands, whose intersections with the second curve give that count. This finite construction uses the supplied drawing and does not use a link-diagram invariance theorem. Summing over all bands and restoring rational coefficients gives $\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)=\sum_e\epsilon_e a_e^2$.

By [F3] and the retraction in step 1.1, a homology class has a unique graph cycle vector. Thus $q(a)=\epsilon\sum_e a_e^2$ is a well-defined quadratic form on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, and step 3.1 proves the required normal-transfer formula for every representative. If $a\ne0$, some edge coefficient is nonzero, so $\sum_ea_e^2>0$. Therefore $q$ is positive definite if $\epsilon=1$ and negative definite if $\epsilon=-1$.

If the connected diagram has no crossings, it is a single circle. Either complementary disk is an embedded connected spanning disk with $H_1=0$. Every cycle in that disk bounds there and has zero linking with its normal transfer, so the zero-dimensional form has the asserted formula and definiteness. This also covers the zero-dimensional cycle space of a Tait tree in the preceding case.
